Bachelor Biologie

Wat te verwachten

Feiten & cijfers
  • Natuur, Gezondheid, Klimaat
  • Fulltime
  • 3 jaar
  • Nederlands
  • Wageningen
Meld je aan

Past deze bachelor bij mij?

Over

Ben jij nieuwsgierig naar alles wat leeft in de natuur, van de kleinste cel tot complete ecosystemen? In Wageningen vormt de groene omgeving een bron van kennis. Daarnaast duik je regelmatig het lab in voor onderzoek. Met persoonlijke begeleiding en veel keuze om je eigen pad te bepalen, floreer jij zeker weten bij de opleiding Biologie.

 

Benieuwd? Kom het zelf ervaren tijdens een proefstudeerdag.

Proefstuderen

Ontdek de opleiding Biologie bij Wageningen University & Research!

Wat maakt deze opleiding uniek?

Brede focus op levenswetenschappen

Je begint breed zodat je ontdekt wat je leuk vindt. Daarna kies je uit het grootste aanbod biologiegerelateerde vakken van Nederland. 

Onderzoek in de natuur en hightech labs

Van veldwerk in bossen tot experimenten in ultramoderne laboratoria op de groene campus van Wageningen.

Studeren midden in de natuur

Vanaf de groene campus fiets je zo naar naar de Veluwe, de uiterwaarden of de Wageningse Hooilanden.

Ontdek je eigen expertise

Je bepaalt je eigen studiesamenstelling. Het onderzoek in? Meewerken aan nieuwe vaccins? Ecosystemen in Zuid-Amerika weer tot leven brengen? Ga ervoor! 

Dit ga je leren

Jouw focus

Je onderzoekt hoe leven functioneert op alle niveaus, van molecuul tot ecosysteem. Je combineert theorie met veel praktijkervaring in veld en laboratorium. 

Dit ga je leren

  • Basisvakken: celbiologie, ecologie, evolutie, genetica, dierbiologie en plantbiologie.
  • Steunvakken: wiskunde, statistiek, scheikunde, natuurkunde.
  • Vaardigheden: presenteren, academisch schrijven, verantwoord AI-gebruik, onderzoeksmethoden in lab en veld.
  • Onderwerpen: klimaatverandering, gezondheid, biodiversiteit, systeembiologie en modelleren.
  • Praktijkervaring: excursies, veldwerk en laboratoriumpractica.
Ontvang de brochure
Belangrijk:
Deze studie richt zich niet op geneeskunde of ziekenhuiszorg, maar je kan je wel richten op de gezondheid en ziekte van mens, dier en plant.

Jouw vakken

Studieprogramma

In het eerste jaar maak je kennis met alle richtingen van de biologie. Je krijgt bijvoorbeeld les over ecologie, cellen, dieren en genetica. Je krijgt ook basisvakken over wiskunde, natuurkunde en scheikunde. Ook leer je presenteren, onderzoek doen, samenwerken en wetenschappelijk schrijven.

Bekijk alle vakken.

In je tweede studiejaar verken je nog meer vakgebieden binnen de biologie. Aan het eind van het jaar mag je je specialiseren. Je kiest jouw favorieten uit een lijst van verdiepende biologische vakken, bijvoorbeeld dierkunde, microbiologie, plantkunde of biologische computermodellen. Er is van alles mogelijk. Daarnaast leer je ook werken met DNA, RNA en eiwitten in het lab.

Bekijk alle vakken.

Dit jaar volg je je laatste specialiserende vak. Daarna mag je vrije keuzevakken volgen. Deze mogen over biologie gaan, maar ook over hele andere onderwerpen zoals datawetenschap of educatie. Je kan vakken volgen in Wageningen, maar ook aan een andere universiteit in Nederland of zelfs in het buitenland. 

Een paar voorbeelden van studenten die vakken in het buitenland hebben gevolgd: 

  • Vakken over meteorologie en geologie in Polen.
  • Vakken over biotechnologie en kanker in Hongkong.
  • Vakken over mariene ecosystemen en klimaatverandering in Canada.

Ook doe je een eigen wetenschappelijk onderzoek van 4 maanden over een thema dat jij interessant vindt. Je maakt een onderzoeksplan, voert je onderzoek uit in het lab of buiten in de natuur, schrijft een wetenschappelijk verslag en presenteert je resultaten aan medestudenten.

Voorbeelden van thesisonderwerpen:

  • Hoe werken de zuignappen van octopussen, en kunnen we dit principe namaken voor menselijke toepassingen?
  • Wat gebeurt er met de stofwisseling en wortelgroei van planten bij droogtestress?
  • Welk effect hebben omgevingsfactoren op het microbioom in onze darmen?

Bekijk alle vakken.

In je derde jaar heb je ruimte om te kiezen voor vakken die jij interessant vindt. Dit kan een minor zijn (vast pakket aan vakken), maar het kunnen ook losse vakken zijn. Een paar voorbeelden van minors:

  • Marine Living Resources
  • Data Science
  • Psychobiology of Eating Behaviour
  • Molecular Life Sciences
  • Earth and Biosphere

Je kunt een minor volgen in Nederland of in het buitenland. Je studieadviseur helpt je om keuzes te maken die bij jou passen.

Bekijk alle minors in dit overzicht. 

 De studie bestaat uit: 

  • Hoorcolleges: een docent legt de lesstof klassikaal uit.
  • Werkcolleges: je maakt opdrachten onder begeleiding van een docent.
  • Groepswerk: samen met een projectgroep voer je een opdracht uit, met of zonder docent.
  • Lab- en computerpractica: je voert experimenten uit in het lab of werkt met modellen, simulaties en data-analyses.
  • Veldpractica/excursies: je leert alles over veldwerk en gaat zelf buiten op onderzoek.
  • Zelfstudie: ingepland in je rooster of op momenten die jij kiest.  

Bij WUR krijg je veel persoonlijke begeleiding. Je hebt meer contact met docenten, studieadviseurs en begeleiders dan bij andere universiteiten. Dat vergroot je kans op succes én maakt studeren leuker. Zo laten we zien dat we echt betrokken zijn bij jouw ontwikkeling.

Sommige bacheloropleidingen lijken wat op elkaar. De belangrijkste gemene deler is dat de genoemde opleidingen bijna allemaal ingaan op een specifieker gebied van de biologie, en de toepassingen in de maatschappij. Terwijl de opleiding Biologie breder is en gaat over het begrijpen van het leven van cel tot ecosysteem.

  • Bachelor Marine Sciences
    Bij Marine Sciences leer je duurzame oplossingen te bedenken voor de oceanen door natuurwetenschappen en maatschappijwetenschappen te combineren.  Bij Biologie richt je je puur op de natuurwetenschappen en kijk je niet alleen naar de oceanen, maar naar allerlei verschillende omgevingen.
  • Bachelor Bos- en Natuurbeheer
    Bos- en Natuurbeheer gaat over de ecologische en maatschappelijke aspecten van het beheer van natuurgebieden en bossen. Bij Biologie kijk je naast ecologie ook naar andere schaalniveau’s zoals cellen en organismen, en richt je je niet op maatschappelijke aspecten.
  • Bachelor Plantenwetenschappen
    Bij Plantenwetenschappen leer je over plantkunde in combinatie met gezondheid, techniek en onderzoek. Bij Biologie kijk je niet alleen naar planten, maar ook naar dieren, bacteriën, schimmels, etc.
  • Bachelor Animal Sciences 
    Bij Animal Sciences, een Engelstalige bachelor, leer je over dieren in relatie tot onze maatschappij. Bij Biologie richt je je meer op dieren in het wild, en leer je ook over andere organismen zoals planten. 

Er zijn meer opleidingen in Wageningen die een link hebben met biologie, zoals Biotechnologie, Moleculaire Levenswetenschappen en Voeding & Gezondheid.  

Benieuwd hoe deze studie het doet vergeleken met andere studies? Check de cijfers op Studiekeuze123.

Je leven na deze bachelor

Na de bachelor

Met de opleiding Biologie kan je veel kanten op:

  • Onderzoeker bij een universiteit of een onderzoeksinstelling als het RIVM of het Nederlands Kanker Instituut.
  • Specialist of adviseur bij vraagstukken over biologie bij gemeentes of bedrijven.
  • Docent op een universiteit, hogeschool of middelbare school.
  • Projectleider of voorlichter bij organisaties zoals Stichting Noordzee of het Wereld Natuur Fonds.

De meeste studenten doen een master na hun bacheloropleiding. Hiermee vergroot je je kennis en ontwikkel je je vaardigheden nog meer. Deze masters sluiten goed aan: 

  • Master Biology
  • Master Aquaculture and Marine Resource Management
  • Master Plant Sciences
  • Master Animal Sciences
  • Master Bioinformatics
  • Master Plant Biotechnology
  • Master Development and Rural Innovation 

Je kunt ook doorstromen naar een andere Wageningse master, bijvoorbeeld Forest and Nature Conservation of Biotechnology. In je derde jaar kies je dan keuzevakken die aansluiten bij het masterprogramma van jouw voorkeur. Je studieadviseur helpt je een route te plannen waarmee je zonder vertraging instroomt. Een master aan een andere universiteit of in het buitenland is vaak ook mogelijk. 

Voorpret en voorbereiding

Handige info

Enthousiast over deze studie? Bij WUR is het aantal plaatsen onbeperkt, er is geen numerus fixus. Bekijk de toelatingseisen voor de bachelor Biologie om te zien of je je direct kunt aanmelden of dat er nog stappen nodig zijn.

Heb je een vwo-diploma met een van deze profielen? Dan kun je je aanmelden. 

  • Natuur en Techniek met Biologie
  • Natuur en Gezondheid met Natuurkunde 
Andere toelatingsmogelijkheden

Heb je geen van de genoemde diploma’s? Dan moet je aantonen dat je vwo-niveau hebt in Engels, Nederlands, Wiskunde A of B, Natuurkunde, Scheikunde en Biologie. Lees hieronder meer wat bij jou van toepassing is: 

  • Vwo-diploma nieuwe tweede fase
  • Hbo-diploma of hbo-propedeuse
  • Uitzonderingen (Colloquium Doctum)
  • Buitenlands diploma

Vragen over aanmelding of toelating? Het Student Service Centre helpt je verder. 

Studeren is helaas niet gratis. Wil je weten welke kosten daarbij komen kijken? Alle informatie over de kosten van deze studie vind je op deze pagina: collegegeld en studiekosten.

Studeren in Wageningen betekent een actieve studentenvereniging, een groene campus en alles op fietsafstand. Wageningen heeft een knusse sfeer en een bruisend studentenleven, met sportclubs, cultuurverenigingen en studiegerelateerde activiteiten. Ontdek alles over het studentenleven in Wageningen.

Students choose a subject for their BSc thesis. At first, they write a research plan for a laboratory, field, and/or data science/modelling study, which they present to their fellow students. Next, students carry out their research plan in which new data are generated. A scientific article is written to present the results of their research. Moreover, students present the results of their work to fellow students. And finally, they defend the thesis, and development of research competencies, in a discussion at the chair group, in which results and conclusions are placed in the wider context of the scientific field. Besides this, students will also reflect on their personal learning goals and development in three academic skills (scientific writing, presenting and collaboration) as part of the BSc Biology Skills Portfolio (YBI38400).

Education of Wildlife Ecology and Conservation

The Wildlife Ecology and Conservation Group is involved in teaching several courses as shown below. Additionally you can do an internship or thesis at our department.

Looking for a thesis or internship?

You are more than welcome to join the on-campus presentations of your fellow students, which will give you a great insight in projects at our group! All research and education at the Wildlife Ecology and Conservation Group is conducted in accordance with the Netherlands Code of Conduct for Scientific Practice.

BSc thesis

BSc Thesis

The lecturers of our group welcome you to carry out your BSc thesis under their supervision.

For more information regarding the rules and orientations for the BSc thesis, consult the website of the BSc theses for Forestry and Nature Conservation students or for Biology students. The idea is that you come up with a theme for the content of the thesis yourself, and contacts one of our staff members asking them to supervise you. But whom to contact? They best way is to visit our people page and check who fits your topic best. Feel free to contact the BSc thesis coordinator or any of our staff to discuss the possibilities.

Choosing a good topic for your BSc thesis is an important first step. We can assist you with that step with these three suggestions:

  1. Have a look at the MSc thesis topics we supervise and the projects of the Staff and PhD researchers. These give you a good impression of the projects we carry out and of our scientific focus.
  2. View this selection of BSc Thesis topics that have been written under our supervision; maybe it can help you in finding another topic?
  3. We have some ideas ourselves for themes that could be used for a BSc thesis. These change continuously and are best discussed directly with one of the staff members.

MSc thesis & internship

MSc thesis & internship

For more information about a MSc internship or thesis at WEC, please see the WEC thesis & internship Brightspace page.

As a student you should first enroll yourself to the discoverable 'course' in Brightspace named 'Thesis and Internship Wildlife Ecology and Conservation'. Follow these instructions: How to find a course using Discover.

Enroll in Brightspace for more information

MSc thesis

MSc Thesis

This WEC thesis & internship Brightspace page (enroll first, see above) contains all the information you need about a thesis or internship at WEC. There, you will also find all documents and forms required for starting a thesis project at WEC.

The MSc-thesis offers the challenge to demonstrate your ability to set up and to carry out a scientific research project in a self-responsible and independent manner.

Find a thesis at WEC: topics BSc/MSc thesis & internships or contact the WEC MSc thesis coordinator.

An overview of our thesis (and internship) topics can be found at MSc thesis and internship topic list. (If this link does not work, please send an e-mail to: thesis.wec@wur.nl).

This challenge includes to:

  • provide an adequate delineation and definition of your research topic,
  • build a sound theoretical framework for orientation of the research,
  • generate proper research questions and/or testable hypotheses,
  • generate proper research questions and/or testable hypotheses,
  • develop methodology fit for hypothesis testing,
  • collect data in a systematic and verifiable manner,
  • analyse the data critically and correctly,
  • present the results in a comprehensible manner,
  • draw sound conclusions based on a comprehensive discussion of the results,
  • show the contribution of your results to the development of the research topic.

Colloquium and thesis ring

A presentation or colloquium is a part of every MSc research project carried out at our group. These presentations are ideal to improve your presentation skills, and to discuss your findings, experimental set-up and conclusions with fellow students and staff.

Colloquia

Online colloquia are organized each Monday afternoon, from 15.30 - 17.30 h. If you plan to hold your colloquium the following steps should be taken:

  • Discuss and schedule a date with your supervisor
  • Prepare an invitation text, mentioning your name, title of the presentation and an abstract. A format is available through your supervisor. This will be used in the invitation to members and students of our group.

For any other questions, please check with the colloquium coordinator or your supervisor!

Thesis rings

Our group hosts several thesis rings. Some are focussed on a specific topic, other on skills such as scientific writing or presenting. Please check with your supervisor what the options are.

Internship

MSc Internship

The internship is a required element of the MSc program. You will be based as an intern at an organisation outside of Wageningen University. This organisation could be a research institute or a consultancy, an NGO or any other organisation where people work on ecological topics. It could be based in Wageningen, elsewhere in The Netherlands, or even abroad. In case you plan to do your internship abroad, check the WUR travel policy for students.

We prefer to organize the internship after you have fulfilled all requirements of your MSc including your MSc major thesis at the Wildlife Ecology and Conservation Group, so that you have the best background and the largest experience that will make the internship a success for you and your receiving organization.

It is customary that you yourself identify your own internship topic and provider. This is often done by writing an email including a cover letter with a motivation and a CV. Applications are more successful if your motivation and previous experience is highlighted clearly. Since topics available at organisations change all the time, it is impossible for the research group to provide an up to date list of available topics. Only in rare cases the Wildlife Ecology and Conservation Group is asked by an internship provider to facilitate in finding a suitable student for a certain topic.

Once you have identified a suitable topic, it is good to contact a WEC staff member well in advance to supervise your internship from the side of the University. It is your responsibility to find a suitable WEC supervisor. If you fail to find somebody, you can contact the Internship coordinator from WEC. The WEC supervisor can help you in shaping your internship to your desires and increase the quality of your internship, and checks whether the suggested topic fulfils the minimum requirements of an academic internship. The day-to-day supervision is, however, taken care of by the internship provider.

Types of internships

There are two varieties of the internship. In a research internship, you work on a single research project that is completed with a research report. In a professional internship, you contribute to different projects. You complete the professional internship with a set of deliverables and a context report.

Pick your internship provider carefully. If you aspire a career in academia, it may be better to do your internship at a research institute or other university which increases chances to obtain a PhD candidacy. The nature of such an internship would therefore be almost equivalent to an MSc thesis. In such cases it is useful to consider the possibility of swapping the internship for a minor MSc thesis. Ask your study advisor for the procedure. The advantage in the latter case is that your WEC supervisor will be able to supervise you more intensively.  If you aspire a career outside of academia, look for possibilities at consultancy's, NGO's etc. This is the chance to build a valuable network. It is not uncommon that internship students are offered a (temporary) job after completion of their internship.

On Brightspace, you can find a list of internship providers where students have done their internship in the past, contacts within those organisations, and contacts within the Wildlife Ecology and Conservation Group.

Education of Laboratory of Molecular Biology

The Laboratory of Molecular Biology is involved in teaching several courses as shown below. Additionally you can do a thesis in our laboratory or an internship somewhere else under supervision of one of our staff members.

Thesis projects for BSc and MSc students

BSc & MSc thesis

The Laboratory of Molecular Biology offers a broad range of thesis projects for BSc and MSc students which are embedded in ongoing state-of-the-art research lines. 

For more information about thesis or internship possibilities or general questions, you can also contact one of our thesis and internship coordinators or send an email to thesis.mob-clb@wur.nl. Please indicate in your message whether you are looking for a MSc or BSc thesis, your study program, period that you would like to start, and the desired amount of credits.

The majority of the course consists of laboratory practical. We work in 6 themes: DNA, RNA, Recombinant DNA technology, proteins, 3D Structure & function and protein complexes. Lectures provide the theoretical background on these themes and the techniques used during the lab practical are also discussed in theoretical e-learning modules. The practical are dedicated to analysis of DNA, RNA and proteins, both from prokaryotes (E. coli) and eukaryotes (tomato). They include isolation of DNA, RNA and proteins, construction of a physical map of a plasmid, cloning and detection techniques like PCR and western blotting. the study of protein function and enzyme kinetics, analysis of protein 3D structure using computer graphics and the discovery of cellular protein complexes with proteomics. Students will also learn basic skills for the use of computer programs and internet tools in the analysis of structure and function of DNA and proteins (bio-informatics). Rubisco will serve as a model in the majority of the experiments. At the end of the experiments students will report about their results and conclusions. The course is concluded with an theoretical exam.

The maximal capacity for this course is limited, both in periods 4 and 5. Note: This course can not be combined in an individual program with PBR34303 Genomics and Bioinformatics.

Over the last decades, a number of technologies to study DNA, RNA, proteins, metabolites and their interactions has been developed. To understand life at the molecular level, they have been applied in numerous biological and biomedical experiments. Much of the resulting data, as well as the knowledge gained in these experiments, are freely available for researchers in the form of computer databases and tools. Analysis and interpretation of experimental data in biology increasingly depends on using these bioinformatics methods efficiently and effectively. In this course, students will be given a broad overview of the field of bioinformatics, with a focus on practical application and interpretation of results from tools used in everyday biological research.

Physics, being a mathematical science, is being presented here as a tool to study biological phenomena. The emphasis is put on a handful of basic underlying principles and their use when trying to solve a diversity of problems from the realistic practice. The topics comprise basic optics (related to vision and microscopy), the kinematics in one and two dimensions, dynamics, statics, hydrostatics and flow phenomena, kinetic theory of gases, thermal motion, diffusion, temperature and heat, calorimetry and phase changes, the steady state transfer of heat by conduction, convention and radiation.
Treating each of the above topics includes a descriptive survey of the basic physical concepts followed by a number of illustrative applications with a sufficient amount of biological details.

The course consists of a botanical and zoological part of two weeks each. Students will learn how to identify higher plants and arthropods using diagnostic keys. Students will also be exposed to the diversity of mammals, birds and amphibians. They will also be expected to recognize a limited number of important taxa on sight. The identification of organisms will take place both during practicals and field excursions. To facilitate an understanding of biodiversity, assignments will be carried out both during practicals and field excursions. The field assignments will focus on making assessments and comparisons of plants and animals in certain areas and habitats. Students will gain knowledge about (woody) plant and arthropod morphology, nomenclature, classification, phylogenetic relationships, habitats, flora districts and the applicability of all of these to ecological studies. Moreover, this connectedness is an essential attribute, at the level of populations, communities and ecosystems.
Food webs are descriptions of biological communities focusing on trophic interactions between consumers and resources. This way, trophic interactions represent pathways in the cycling of matter, energy and nutrients. Food web interactions significantly influence the dynamics and persistence of populations by determining the availability of resources and mortality rates due to predation. As a result, food webs are important drivers of biodiversity in ecosystems, and allow to upscale environmental effects from the level of individuals and population to that of ecosystems.
Food webs provide a comprehensive framework for this course, in which you will learn the theoretical background of these webs, as well as practical skills that allow you to dissect them. During field work at a range of sites and habitats in the highly biodiverse French Pyrenees, you will train your recognition and identification skills, by becoming acquainted with morphological traits, and by learning microscopic and DNA-based techniques and be able to measure biodiversity. Second and third year courses that follow are e.g. CBI21303, CBI20803.","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"This course is part of the first year program for Biology, Biotechnology, Molecular Life Sciences, Nutrition and Health and Plant Sciences students. The course content provides necessary knowledge for continuation courses in all these study programs. Cell Biology forms an introductory and partly specialized course into the structure and function of plant, animal and bacterial cells and biomolecules.

Special focus is directed at the ultrastructure and function of the different cell organelles, the cytoskeleton and cellular organization. Furthermore, the molecular and biochemical basis of cell function and cell differentiation processes are discussed. Recent research insights into cellular mechanisms are applied in the course. Basic principles of intra- and extracellular communication processes will be studied to obtain insight into the regulation of cell function in the context of whole tissues, organs and complete organisms. Every week has a theme and in relation to this theme there will be a practical and a group discussion. During practicals students explore, among others, mitosis and meiosis in plant and animal cells, transcriptional regulation in bacteria and the role of membranes in cell homeostasis (e.g. vacuoles, cholesterol, receptors, channels and transporters). Additionally, there is a case integrating the topics of that weeks, such as pharmaceutical compounds of plants, role of neurotransmitters in depression and regulation of cell cycles.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Every week is started with a new theme.This is introduced during plenary lectures. Theory is supported by ICT modules. Subsequently students work in small groups of 12 students wherein they are offered case studies with specific tasks that have to be prepared during the week and presented in mandatory group discussions at the end of each week. Cases should challenge the students to analyse the related subjects in the light of the weekly theme. If a mandatory group meeting is missed due to valid reason a replacing assignment can be requested by the course coordinator. The weekly learning goals comprise the knowledge needed to understand and explain the case. Laboratory practicals are a mandatory part of the course. The biological assays

chosen are related to the weekly theme as well as the cases under study. Techniques applied are microscopy and cell biological analyses, supported by computer modules and short movies. Practical reports provide basic skills in scientific writing.

The immune system refers to a collection of cells and proteins that function to protect the skin, respiratory tract, intestinal tract from initial pathogen entry and our entire system from pathogen-mediated damage such as from microbes (organisms such as bacteria fungi, and parasites), viruses but also cancer cells. Recent advances in translational, clinical and fundamental research provide evidence for the modulation of immune responses (e.g. by foods, dietary ingredients and natural products). The purpose of the Introduction to Human Immunology course is to provide a basic knowledge of the immune response and the mechanisms by which humans, but principles and processes apply to other mammals as well, defend themselves against foreign antigens.

The course will focus on:

  • basic aspects of immunology; the innate and adaptive immune system
  • immune cell interactions to maximize, but also limit, immune responses
  • immune-related disorders in humans
  • experimental laboratory assays enabling detection of immunomodulatory activity

This course overlaps with CBI21303. Therefore, combing this course with CBI21303 is not allowed.

This course centers around the book by Sompayrac entitled 'how the immune system works'. This book provides the basics on immunology by describing functionality of individual cells and specific key functions of the immune system in a very engaging manner as the author is 'talking' to the readers. The lectures are constructed to complement the book by describing the key concepts of immunology and after this applying these key concepts to explain how the immune system and certain key immune cells work. The students will apply their newly gained knowledge on how the immune system works during two guest lectures and a tutorial that all describe a disease state and in practicals where students will examine activities of specific cell types.


The tutorial is designed for students to understand a disease state from initiation to pathology. For this tutorial students are expected to critically read scientific articles on a specific topic (Celiac Disease, Diabetes or Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)) and answer questions via brightspace. The brightspace module is designed to engage the student and question their understanding, but also test efficient and effectieve reading/scanning of articles and provide additional insights and learnings.


The practicals are scheduled on four consecutive mornings during which students will learn to perform basic laboratory techniques and biological assays (pipetting) through which they will illustrate activities of the innate immune system by identifying macrophage responses, and illustrate activities of the adaptive immune system by testing cytotoxic T cell responses and demonstrating antibody specificity and function. The first two biological assays are accompanied by a labbuddy-based test to demonstrate, instruct and educate students on how to properly describe an aim, result section, discussion and conclusion (which information is shared in which section and how to be as complete as necessary and short as possible). Based on the third biological assay the students will write a short report including the aim, results, discussion and conclusion.


The exam will be a computer based examination with questions on the lectures, tutorials and practicals at the end of the period.

","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"Sexual reproduction is one of the major characteristics of eukaryotes and involves a regular alternation between meiosis and fertilization. This course focuses on the basic principles of plant reproduction and the evolution of reproductive strategies in mosses, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms. This knowledge is used as basis to understand the concepts that underlie sexual reproduction in dicot and monocot angiosperm species. Topics including flower induction, flower development, fertilization, embryogenesis, seed development and dispersal, and fruit-development are covered.
This course aims to develop insight into evolutionary, regulatory and structural aspects of the reproductive strategies of plants. During the practicals experimental techniques used to obtain insight in structural aspects and developmental processes associated with plant reproduction are taught and practiced. These activities aim to prepare students to independently interpret reproductive strategies of any plant species.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course consists of lectures, practicals and an excursion to arboretum 'De Dreijen\" in Wageningen. prior knowledge assumed.","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Biology as a science informs how we think of ourselves and of our relationship with nature. This course aims to understand the scientific character of contemporary biology, and how it gives influences problems in social ethics, animal ethics, environmental ethics, and the ethics of biotechnology.


There are two parts to the course:

1. Philosophy of science. How does biology explain phenomena, and how does that compare to other sciences (physics, anthropology)? How has this changed over time (from pre- to post-Darwinian biology)? What is the difference with religion, or with pseudo-science? How does biology progress and generate predictive theories? And finally, what are the values of biology as a science, and how is used to inform policy?

2. Ethics. We touch on the concept of \"nature\" and \"human nature\", and discuss how biology informs ethical discussions concerning human behavior, human-animal relations (speciesism, human uniqueness), environmental ethics (anthropocentrism, biocentrism), and biotech (genetic engineering, environmental engineering).

The Zoology course centers on understanding the phenotype of vertebrates, emphasizing the continual adaptations animals make to thrive in their environments. You'll learn how the morphology (form) of tissues, organs, and even entire organisms is closely tied to their functions. We begin with the relationship between ontogeny (embryonic development) and phylogeny (evolutionary history), using the EVO-DEVO model. This framework enables us to explore the fundamental ancestral blueprint (bauplan) of vertebrates, such as the shark, alongside the specialized adaptations required for diverse lifestyles.

The course then progresses to examine structure, function, and regulation within the vertebrate body, applying integrative and comparative approaches. Key organ systems, including the skin, skeleton, muscles, and nervous system, will be covered, while others—such as the respiratory, circulatory, reproductive, and endocrine systems—will be addressed in the following course, Human and Animal Physiology (HAP20306). The vertebrate phenotype is further contextualized within behavioral, ecological, and life-history strategies.

In the laboratory, students will explore vertebrate structure and function both macroscopically and microscopically. This includes a full anatomical exploration of a key vertebrate species with a special focus on the brain, along with histological analyses of vertebrate skin, muscles, and bones. In vivo physiological experiments will help illuminate how different systems integrate through sensor-integration-effector pathways. Several sessions will also incorporate digital learning tools for added support and insight.


NOTE: This course contains some practical work involving dissection. According to the Student Charter, based on conscientious objections, a dissection-free variant can be offered within this same course code. Registration for this variant is only possible by requesting this by email from the course coordinator prior to the course registration deadline. It requires consultation with, and approval from the course coordinator of this course.

This course elaborates on the basic mechanisms of development that were introduced in ‘Mechanisms of development’ (MOB20803). Although plants and animals have developed separately for about 1.6 billion years, an ‘overall logic of development’ can be found when plants and animals are compared. In this course we will deepen our understanding of the mechanisms that underlie plant and animal development. We will use several of the mathematical tools that were introduced in ‘Modeling biological systems’ (EZO23306) to derive a more quantitative description of several developmental mechanisms. Such a quantitative description is required to properly interpret the possibilities and impossibilities of the mechanisms underlying plant and animal development.

The course is designed around six major themes. The first theme is from polarization to gradient formation. In early development, axes are determined in an initially mostly symmetrical embryo. This polarization (or symmetry-breaking) leads to the formation of gradients of signalling molecules. Concentration gradients of these morphogens are crucial to a proper interpretation of the signal. During this theme we will elaborate on Drosophila development, which we first saw in ‘Mechanisms of development’, and analyse the mathematical key concepts of gradient formation. Furthermore, we will see how an auxin gradient is formed and maintained during plant root growth.

The second theme is gene network inference. Animal and plant development needs to be regulated, and genes are the producers of regulators such as transcription factors and morphogens. Genes do not function individually, but are part of networks. These networks often have a modular structure and regulate a specific part of development. In this second theme we will see how networks are formed and maintained and we will see examples of how networks regulate development. Artificial intelligence will be used to infer a gene network.

Polar growth mechanisms comprise the third theme. We met polarity already in ‘Mechanisms of development’, when we discussed the early steps of Xenopus development. The Xenopus egg showed a clear polarity with a heavily pigmented animal pole and a clear vegetal pole. During this course we will focus on polarity later in development, and in association with cell movement in a particular direction (i.e. polar growth). Gene networks and gradients play an important role in the regulation of the cell’s actin skeleton. We will see how keratocytes are polarized and how they are able to move. In plants, we will try to understand tip growth in roots and pollen tubes.

In the fourth theme dynamic control of pattern formation, we will combine gradients, gene networks, and polarity to understand how detailed patterns are dynamically controlled. We will discover that the mechanism of lateral inhibition plays a crucial role in both the formation of somites in animals, and the formation of root hairs in plants. It will further become clear that communication between cells is essential to pattern formation.

The fifth theme is self-organising multicellularity. In this theme you will be introduced to the slime molds, such as Dictyostelium discoideum. This organism provides an interesting example of multicellular organization derived from unicellular organisms in a single life cycle. Plants and animals have also made the transition from unicellular to multicellular organism, albeit over millions of years of evolution. We will see how the previous themes integrate to explain the social reproductive cycle of Dictyostelium.

The sixth theme is regeneration. Regeneration is a process that is still poorly understood, but it integrates many of the aspects treated in the previous themes as well as many of the topics from ‘Mechanisms of development’. We will try to understand the current state of knowledge and possibly formulate hypothesis on how and why this intriguing phenomenon is so evidently working in amphibians and not in mammals.

The general setup of the course is that each theme is studied by two special topics. Where possible, one of the topics relates to plant development and the other to animal development.

Biological systems are arguably the most complex systems science tries to understand. We make observations, and try to obtain useful insight in the systems. This requires hypotheses; ideas of how we believe the world around us is structured and operates. Models translate our hypotheses into concrete predictions about our objects of study that can be tested by targeted experiments.

The more complex the systems we study, the more crucial the use of models. The SARS-CoV2 outbreak is an example of a highly complex biological system. Models of how this virus spreads are crucial because they provide predictions that in turn can be used to take appropriate measures. Without models, we would not be able to focus the measures to combat this virus. There is a key role for one of the strongest tools in our scientific toolkit: mathematics. Mathematics are able to capture complexity in a form that makes it manageable. Mathematical models allow a full exploration of the consequences of our hypotheses and provide quantitative, and therefore precisely testable, predictions. Nowadays, this modelling toolkit is vastly extended by the wide availability of computers, which allow us to implement and test mathematical models, or even directly simulate the behaviour of complex systems.

In this course we attempt to convey the fascination for biological systems and introduce the tools to model them.

Mondays start with self study using knowledge clips and the theory manual. The combination of both introduces the tools needed to do the tutorials later that week. After the self-study, a plenary lecture is scheduled. In the first week, this lecture serves as an introduction to the course. In the following weeks, the lectures focus on applying the theory in different contexts and thus prepare you for the exam.

Tuesdays start with an introductory meeting per group. The rest of the Tuesday morning is a tutorial during which you work with your two partners on the exercises of that week.

Wednesdays start with a meeting per group where the progress of the previous day can be discussed. Then the tutorial is continued and you again work in subgroups on the exercises of that week.

Thursdays also start with a meeting per group, followed by work on the exercises during the tutorial in subgroups. At the end of each Thursday the exercises should be finished. In weeks 3 to 6 you hand in your Jupyter notebook with answers as a subgroup.

Fridays are dedicated for exam training. In weeks 1 and 2 you will make an interim Python test that is graded individually. In weeks 3 to 6 you work on your own pet project as a group. The last Friday a poster fair is organised to present the results of your pet project.

Notes

  • This course is divided over two periods (5 & 6) and includes a field course. The course can only be completed in the correct order (first P5 then P6). Participation in the field course is not allowed without completing the program in Wageningen.
  • As postulated in the student charter a contribution must be paid to cover the cost of living during the field course.


In this course we study how have algae, fungi and invertebrate animals are adapted in structure, function, and behaviour to survive and reproduce in a wide spectrum of biotic and abiotic conditions. Next to that we also practice a set of skills that are important for the rest of your study (e.g. BSc-thesis) and your future career.

The questions about of Invertebrates, algae and fungi are discussed on phylogenetic and ontogenetic time scales. This provides insight in biodiversity, evolutionary theory and the social and economic importance of these groups. Following lectures, histological, dissection and other lab-exercises, all questions are finally integrated in a field course where invertebrate animals and algae are studied in their natural habitat of the intertidal zone (normally in Wimereux, France). There we can explore the adaptations and constraints of these highly diverse organisms, and their interactions in a natural community. You are also trained in doing research in a field work setting, and will practice some of the academic skills mentioned below.

Skills that will be incorporated in this course are all important for an doing research and can be seen as a preparation for the BSc-thesis and future careers. Participants will write a scientific paper about a research project performed in the same period. Participants will be trained in, and practice with, the use of information resources (library, internet sites, AI and portals) to optimize the writing. In addition students will get the chance to improve their papers based on feedback from reviewers as customary when submitting papers for publication. Students will practice communication skills by presenting their own findings to the rest of the group in different settings. During the field-course we will focus on skills for working in a scientific environment. Skills will include: maintaining a labjournal, feedback, teamwork, presenting, and writing skills.


NOTE: This course contains some practical work involving dissection. According to the Student Charter, based on conscientious objections, a dissection-free variant can be offered within this same course code. Registration for this variant is only possible by requesting this by email from the course coordinator prior to the course registration deadline. It requires consultation with, and approval from the course coordinator of this course.

In Wageningen:

  • Lectures and lab-exercises on the subject of invertebrate biology, algae, and fungi integrated with theoretical issues, including self-tests.
  • Participants present information on invertebrates in an oral presentations to improve presentation skills and giving feedback to fellow students.
  • Participants will write and improve a paper based on scientific research and comments from reviewers.
  • Participants will make two assignments using the library network to extend their information resource skills.
  • Participants will get an introduction in responsible AI-use.

During the field work in Wimereux:

  • General training and practice in fieldwork, appropriate time management, teamwork and feedback.
  • During low tide you will characterise (in biotic and physical sense) selected field locations.
  • Observed species are studied by small groups of students and analysed for taxonomy, structure, function, lifestyle, and biological role.
  • Eventually, 'simple' experiments exploring adaptation of animals and algae are designed and performed. The whole experiment should be recorded showing adequate skills in lab-journal use.
  • The results of a selection of the assignments are presented to fellow participants in several settings.
  • During the field course observations and results have to be recorded in a field journal, including a selection of writing assignments.

","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

All living organisms have evolved and continue to do so. Evolutionary biology studies the history of that process and the mechanisms that cause it to happen. This introductory course treats microevolution (the evolutionary changes occurring within populations and species over a limited number of generations), organismal design by selection for reproductive success, and macroevolution (the evolution of new species and the long-term evolutionary changes above the species level). It distinguishes between the two general methodologies to study evolution: the direct experimental study of processes (often using microbes in the laboratory) and the comparative method that interprets relatedness patterns among now-living organisms to test hypotheses. These are the specific themes and subthemes that will be treated: microevolutionary concepts, population genetics, design by selection for reproductive success, principles of macroevolution, the history of life, integrating micro- and macroevolution.

- Additional learning activities include watching a movie introducing Darwin's ideas, the collection of your own ancestral data, an excursion to Naturalis with \"field-work assignment\", and weekly lunch discussion meetings on topics of choice.

Have you ever wondered how you can:

  • determine the origin of wolves crossing the Dutch border?
  • find out what bears eat, even if you only have access to their poo?
  • determine the region of origin of invasive insect pest species threatening fruit production?
  • find out how you can get information from DNA sampled at a crime site?


If you are interested in ecology and evolution and want an answer to these types of questions, the Molecular and Evolutionary Ecology (MEE) course GEN-20306, is just the course for you!
The subject of the MEE course is the application of molecular techniques and evolutionary concepts for ecological research, which will be illustrated and applied in a personal experimental research project. The course starts with a practical training in molecular techniques like DNA isolation, RFLP and PCR analysis and gel-electrophoresis and focuses on its use for answering ecological and evolutionary questions. Mini-projects will be introduced in the second week. The mini-projects are organized in research teams, each consisting of 4-5 groups that will work on their own research questions centred around one of 6 overarching research topics. The last two weeks will be used to finish the course (written reports, oral presentations at the final symposium and an oral final evaluation).

","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"The course introduces Geo-Information Science and its scientific and societal interests. The starting point of the introduction is the geo-information cycle. This cycle frames geo data based actions like acquisition and storage, processing and visualization. It is explained that these actions can be used to describe, to analyse, to design and to realize real world phenomena. Thus geo data is always acquired, processed and visualized with a specific purpose. This is illustrated via the conceptual, formal and technical modelling steps.
Important in these modelling steps are the roles of geographical data attributes (thematic, geometric, temporal). Because the acquisition and processing of geo data is purposive, meta data plays an important role to find geo data and geo data processing steps. It also is important to evaluate the (re)usability of geo data and geo data processing steps. Meta data explain important geo data characteristics like (geo)reference, map projection and available attributes. Geo-visualization, especially cartography concepts, is introduced to show how geo data ought to be communicated. After the introduction of the geo data related concepts, the course offers the geo data processing options. The latter is done by the introduction of three data handling classes (query, transform and alter) and the data-action model. The geo data that represent terrain height and processing of these elevation data has given notice. Besides, basic concepts of Remote Sensing (spectral signature, sensor types, visual and quantitative processing) are also introduced. The application of all concepts is practiced during a practical and by a small project using professional software and data according a working procedure.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

Human and Animal Physiology is a 6 credits course that is closely related to the course Zoology (EZO10306 for BBI students and EZO10806 for BAS students) and continues on the functioning of organ systems. All these organ systems together are critical for all individual mammals to 1) function, 2) be able to maintain its internal environment (within certain limits), and 3) to adapt to the demands of the environment. The course is organized in themes, each theme dealing with metabolism and organ systems at the cellular, tissue and organismal level. The emphasis will be on the relationship between morphology, physiology and regulation of these organ systems. Each theme will be introduced during a lecture explaining the anatomy and physiology of the organ system involved and sometimes focused on certain specific details. The gained knowledge will then be practiced, repeated and deepened during the morphological, histological and physiological practicals. During a case study, the flexibility of the phenotype will be investigated, reported and presented in a poster, and discussed in an informal poster presentation.


NOTE: This course contains some practical work involving dissection. According to the Student Charter, based on conscientious objections, a dissection-free variant can be offered within this same course code. Registration for this variant is only possible by requesting this by email from the course coordinator prior to the course registration deadline. It requires consultation with, and approval from the course coordinator of this course.

Physiology.","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

This course is focused on the physiological utilisation of dietary macro-nutrients (carbohydrates, fat and protein) and discusses their flow from oral intake to their utilisation and/or excretion under various physiological conditions as maintenance, production, physical activity, stress, etc. Metabolism is discussed as an interface between 'Nutritional Input' and 'Physiological Output' of the body.
This course discusses the main biochemical processes involved in digestion, absorption and cellular metabolism of macro-nutrients.
Special attention will be paid to potential constraints for proper physiological functioning of the body.
The intensity of energy metabolism might have adverse effects on the ability to maintain the body temperature depending on the environmental conditions (thermo-neutral zone, comfort zone). Within protein metabolism there may be a friction between the efficiency of protein utilization for maintenance, protein deposition and the ability to cope with stress conditions as far as mediated by protein turnover.
With regard to (semi)-quantitative aspects relevant for nutritional physiology, specific assignments will be discussed. During practicals, students will study aspects of digestion, absorption and metabolism in both in vivo and in vitro experiments.


NOTE: This course contains some practical work involving dissection. According to the Student Charter, based on conscientious objections, a dissection-free variant can be offered within this same course code. Registration for this variant is only possible by requesting this by email from the course coordinator prior to the course registration deadline. It requires consultation with, and approval from the course coordinator of this course.

To date, there is no field in experimental biology that has remained untouched by the potential of isolating, analyzing and manipulating genes and organisms. Thus, gene technology provides essential tools in both fundamental and applied medical, industrial, agricultural, environmental and biological research.
In this course we will focus on four major topics, including (i) production of transgenic mammals, (ii) altering gene function using knockouts, RNAi and gene editing, (iii) transgenic mice as human model systems and (iv) production of transgenic crops. In addition to conventional lectures that will outline the major procedures, applications and some research papers, students will be challenged by virtual (computer based) experimental designs on the generation and characterization of transgenic animals and plants.
The practical course involves biomolecular techniques to illustrate two experiments.The first one will deal with the identification, characterization and complementation of mutations in organisms. Basic and more advanced gene technology will be applied such as genomic and plasmid DNA isolation, PCR, golden gate cloning, transformation, restriction/digestion and complementation analysis. The second experiment centers on the generation of site specific mutations and gene editing using CRISPR-Cas technology. These experiments will be supported in a virtual environment.
Due to a limited number of places available in the practical part of the course, students are encouraged to register in time. This course deals with the processes that coordinate the development of a single cell into a complex multi-cellular organism. In general, all cells of an organism originate from a single fertilized egg cell, and they share the same set of genes. However, they show differential gene expression and therefore, cells can have different functions within an organism. This course emphasises the molecular mechanisms by which differentiation is induced at the right place and time during development (=pattern formation) and on stem cells. Stem cells have the ability to develop into several -if not all- cell types (pluripotency). During the course, the similarities and differences in plant and animal developmental mechanisms are explained. Mechanisms that control pattern formation in plants as well as in animals are for example:
- the formation of gradients of morphogens that are subsequently translated into distinct regions (tissues) with sharp borders;
- cell communication leading to the induction of a new cell type at the interface;
- noise that, by lateral inhibition, is translated into a pattern.
The underlying molecular mechanisms of such developmental concepts will be explained during the course. For example, how does a morphogen gradient turn on key regulators in distinctive regions, which subsequently affect the expression of target genes, and how can small random differences between cells lead to a typical pattern formation by cell-cell communication?

Emerging infectious diseases of humans and animals make it into the headlines of the news on a daily basis (e.g. malaria, TBC, norovirus). This multidisciplinary course approaches these infectious diseases from several perspectives, including the underlying biology, ecology, epidemiology, and socio-economics. Information will be provided on new insights on the causative agents of several infectious diseases (e.g. viral, prion, bacterial, fungal, protozoan, and parasitic worm diseases) as well as arthropod vector biology and vector-borne diseases. Mathematical modelling has strongly influenced policy-making in relation to the epidemiology and control of infectious diseases. In this course we will focus on the key principles of epidemiological models of infectious diseases to understand how they are used in the health economy.

CBI10306 Celbiology.","type":{"code":"AK","id":"AK","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Assumed knowledge on:"}],"uid":"fdda01e3-c543-4b24-a3cb-9c4690e5a654"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

In their struggle for survival, organisms have to adapt continuously to changes in their abiotic and biotic environment. This course focuses on the molecular mechanisms and consequences of these adaptations for individual organisms and interactions among organisms. Attention will be paid to various (a)biotic conditions and the physiological response of organisms to these conditions, from cellular to organismal level. In particular, we discuss heat-stress and osmotic stress. We also pay attention to the physical properties of the environment and how organisms deal with these properties, for instance in acoustic communication. Finally, we focus on human-induced changes in the environment and how organisms are affected by these changes. Common mechanisms and key concepts across kingdoms underlying adaptation, plasticity, and trade-offs will be analyzed in depth. Examples will be shown how environmental conditions affect signal transduction pathways leading to adaptive changes in ecology, behavior, and phenology.

ENT30306 Ecological Aspects of Biointeractions.","type":{"code":"CC","id":"CC","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Continuation courses:"}],"uid":"45f89e4c-ed7e-493b-b499-b4f953a95118"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

This course is complementary to and runs parallel to Ecology I (PEN10503) and serves to train students in practical investigations of ecological issues and problems. Ecology-2 is specifically set up for first year Bachelor students in Biology and Forest and Nature Conservation and Plant Sciences. The course is given during the 1st and 6th period of the first year. The aim is to learn and understand ecological concepts by performing data-yielding experiments under field, greenhouse and/or laboratory conditions (practical part) and writing a short literature-based project proposal targeting a current ecological problem (project part). The students report their results by means of writing two reports, one for the practical part and one for the project part, as well as a presentation for the project part.

","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

(1) Field and laboratory practicals are carried out in small (2-3 students) groups under the skilled supervision of teaching staff. Dealing with ecological themes like biodiversity, variation in ecosystems, climate and ecosystems, agroecology, life cycles and population dynamics, students identify project aims, collect data, conduct basic data analyses, and report on these, both in writing and orally. The added value here is to solve an ecological problem by means of group activity under supervision of a teacher.
(2) Within the broad setting of ecology, small (ca 5 students) groups each narrow down on a group-specific research question under the skilled supervision of teaching staff. Searching for peer-reviewed and other scientific papers, students write a project proposal with proper scientific framing and phrasing, leading to academic and practical conclusions, backed-up with references. Students present this proposal in a written and an oral form.

The focus is on the form and function relationships with respect to the main functions of the plant. The course consists of a cell biological/structural part (with emphasis on cell structure and organisation, cell division, plant morphogenesis and differentiation) and a physiological part (focussing on e.g. photosynthesis, respiration, water and ion transport, regulation of growth by plant hormones and light, and interaction between plants and micro-organisms). Next to general principles also plant developmental flexibility gets attention, as well as the diversity in the plant kingdom, e.g. differences between monocots and dicots, plants with and without secondary growth, and plants with C3-, C4- or CAM-photosynthesis.

Aims of the course are the creation of a good knowledge of the relationship between structure and function of the various parts of the plant body, including processes that regulate growth and development of plants and their interrelationships. Series of lectures (17) and three practical assignments.

During the lectures the basic principles of toxicology are introduced followed by a discussion on the mode of action of chemicals towards potential adverse effects. Examples of cases relevant for human health will be given. In addition, some examples of environmental toxicology will be provided.
By the practical assignments you will learn to perform laboratory experiments that are frequently used within experimental toxicology for the hazard identification of a chemical. You will work with a fellow student on the experiments, and report on your findings. Next to that you will analyse a more complex toxicological test looking at the developmental toxicity of two compounds. For this a virtual practical is designed in which you will evaluate results obtained using a zebrafish embryo test.
Presence is obligatory for the practical course, and is strongly recommended for the lectures.

The course aims at providing the necessary statistical skills for the data analysis of BSc and MSc thesis projects and will enable the students to be able to understand and critically evaluate the analysis of ecological projects, such as described in scientific publications.","type":{"code":"CO","id":"CO","names":[{"language":"EN","value":"Contents:"}],"uid":"dd16e77e-e3ac-431c-97f2-9a4dae6bb43b"}},{"language":"EN","text":"

This course deals with the choice and application of univariate and multivariate statistical techniques and tests, for the interpretation of ecological field data. The choice of appropriate test will be given attention in relation to the type of data under investigation. The necessary theoretical statistical background is expected to be present. The use of software (R, Excel, Ecological packages) for the analysis of field data will be highlighted and exercised. Attention will be paid to the sequence: hypothesis, choice of tests, interpretation of statistical results, and ecological meaning of outcome with respect to the hypothesis;
- students will attend lectures explaining the general approach of a sound ecological research proposal based on hypothesis testing, and on each of the main statistical techniques. Emphasis will be placed on the use of data from plant-animal interactions and studies on individual plant or animal species;
- introductory lectures will be followed by computer-based exercises to practice the application of statistical techniques to ecological data, where students work in pairs. Some exercises will be discussed interactively with the entire classroom at the end of each practical session, and correct answers will be made available then;
- 7 days of the course are reserved for applied statistics: cluster analysis, survival analysis, species richness analysis, species distribution modelling, time-series analysis, geo-statistics, and capture-recapture data analysis;
- once the main techniques are mastered and tested, student groups will each analyze a large, real-life dataset, using both univariate and multivariate statistical techniques to obtain an ecological interpretation. The ecological datasets are supplied by the lecturers of the course, in co-operation with PhD-students, covering plant, forestry, and animal topics.

This is a longitudinal course spanning all three years of the BSc Biology.

Throughout the BSc programme, students develop essential academic skills such as collaboration, writing and presenting. These skills are practiced across multiple courses and in some courses students receive targeted feedback and formal assessment on their academic performance.

In the BSc Biology Skills Portfolio, students reflect on their progress in academic skills by asking themselves questions such as: Where do I stand now? What am I doing well and what can I improve? This reflection aims to increase self-awareness and encourage personal leadership.

Students are automatically enrolled at the start of their first year of the BSc Biology. The course has to be completed in order to graduate for the BSc Biology.

Students choose a subject for their BSc thesis. At first, they write a research plan for a laboratory, field, and/or data science/modelling study, which they present to their fellow students. Next, students carry out their research plan in which new data are generated. A scientific article is written to present the results of their research. Moreover, students present the results of their work to fellow students. And finally, they defend the thesis, and development of research competencies, in a discussion at the chair group, in which results and conclusions are placed in the wider context of the scientific field. Besides this, students will also reflect on their personal learning goals and development in three academic skills (scientific writing, presenting and collaboration) as part of the BSc Biology Skills Portfolio (YBI38400).

  • in case of emergency: how to respond to emergencies;
  • computer work: how to prevent complaints on arms, neck and shoulder (CANS/ RSI);
  • social safety and being an active bystander.

And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures.
Therefore the Laboratory Safety course is mandatory for all students working in a laboratory environment.

In this course you'll be introduced to working safe in the laboratories of WUR and cover a range of topics for working in our biological and chemical laboratories:

  • General safety while working in the lab
  • Hazardous substances/ chemicals
  • Biological agents

At WUR we value your safety. Going into the field for an excursion or for observations/ measurements exposes you to specific risks some of which you'd take for granted while visiting nature or urban environments outside the university perspective. Things like traffic or uneven terrain seems something that you face on a day to day basis, but need a more strict approach while facing them in a professional way. Furthermore infection prevention and social responsible behavior are topics that require specific attention. Therefore many measures are taken in order to facilitate a safe study in Wageningen.
And although all these measures are in place still one of the most important factors for a safe stay is YOUR behavior and knowledge of these measures. Therefore the Fieldwork Safety course is mandatory for all students going into the field for their education.
This course will introduce you to safe fieldwork during courses at WUR and will cover a range of topics:

  • how to prepare for fieldwork;
  • what risk can you be exposed to when working in the field.

Education of Behavioural Ecology

Education by the Behavioural Ecology Group covers the whole field of animal behaviour, including basic behavioural mechanisms, behavioural ecology, applied animal behaviour, animal welfare and life history decisions. Our courses are directed towards both Biology and Animal Science students.

Thesis

Are you a BSc or MSc student with a fascination for the intricate world of animal behaviour and are you looking for a thesis topic? Explore the thesis opportunities we currently offer, get inspired by browsing through the research topics within our group. Check our Research page or click on the button below. On WUR Career Platform, you can find an overview of our available projects. You need to make an account to check our projects. If you find a topic of your interest, contact the contact person of the project. When you contact one of our staff members about a thesis topic, please wait for their response, before contacting other staff members. If you are interested in doing your thesis at our chair group, but aren't sure about the topic yet, please contact Eline Weenink (Thesis/Internship/RP coördinator).

  • BHE80324 - MSc thesis Behavioural Ecology (24-33 ECTS)
  • BHE80336 - MSc thesis Behavioural Ecology (36 or 39 ECTS)
  • YAS80312 - BSc thesis Animal Sciences
  • YBI85812 - BSc thesis Biology (12 ECTS)
  • YBI86324 - BSc thesis Biology (24 ECTS)

Go to all available thesis topics

Internship & Research practice

Are you an MSc student with an interest in understanding the complex behaviours of animals and their interactions with the environment? And are you looking for an internship or research practice opportunity? The Behavioural Ecology group offers several opportunities for internships and research practices and provides an overview of available and previous internship or research practice topics (see buttons below). On WUR Career Platform, you can find an overview of our available projects. You need to make an account to check our projects. If you found a topic of your interest, contact the contact person of the project. When you contact one of our staff members, please wait for their response, before contacting other staff members. If you found an internship yourself and are looking for a supervisor, please contact Eline Weenink (Thesis/Internship/RP coördinator).

  • BHE70224 - MSc Internship Behavioural Ecology (24-30 ECTS)
  • BHE70324 - MSc Internship Behavioural Ecology (24-36 ECTS)
  • BHE79224 - MSc Research Practice Behavioural Ecology (24-30 ECTS)
  • BHE79324 - MSc Research Practice Behavioural Ecology (24-36 ECTS)

Go to all available internship positions

Questions about theses or internships?

If you are interested in doing your thesis at our chair group, but aren't sure about the topic yet, please contact Eline Weenink (Thesis/Internship/RP coördinator).

EJE (Eline) Weenink

Thesis/Internship/RP coördinator

BHE Tinbergen Thesis prize

Prize

Every year the BHE Tinbergen Thesis prize is awarded. MSc thesis students are eligible when they have a 8 or higher on their thesis. All these theses are read and judged by the committee. The evaluation is based on among other aspects, the quality of abstract, conceptualization, experimental design, figures and embedding in scientific literature. The committee selects a winner and runner-ups.

  • BHE31306 - Applied Animal Behaviour and Welfare - Period 5

  • BHE30306 - Behavioural Ecology - Period 6

The Behavioural Ecology Group of chairholder Marc Naguib studies the causes and consequences of decisions animals make with a focus on social contexts.

Education of Laboratory of Cell and Developmental Biology

The Laboratory of Cell and Developmental Biology is involved in teaching several courses on cell biology; plant morphology, evolution and development; and technologies including light microscopy and tissue culture. You can do an internship or thesis in our laboratory.

Thesis projects for BSc and MSc students

BSc and MSc thesis

The Cell Biology departments offers a broad range of graduation projects for BSc and MSc students which are embedded in ongoing state-of-the-art research lines.

For general questions you can contact our coordinator or send a e-mail to thesis.mob-clb@wur.nl. Please indicate in your message whether you are looking for a MSc or BSc thesis, your study program, period that you would like to start, and the desired amount of credits.
